In the example the largest ID is 5, so candidates are 1–5, of which 2 and 3 never appear. The guarantee that IDs never exceed 100 makes even a repeated full-table scan trivially fast — the exercise is about expressing the "generate candidates, then anti-join" pattern cleanly. Note the upper bound is dynamic: it comes from the data (MAX), not a fixed constant.
k: Generate every candidate ID from 1 to MAX(customer_id) and keep those absent from the table — a generated-series anti-join.
Because max ID ≤ 100, a tiny boolean presence array gives linear time with O(1)-sized state.
SQL has no native number generator, so a recursive CTE supplies the candidate sequence.

a.i: Mirror the statement literally: try every integer from 1 up to the maximum ID and scan the table to see whether it occurs. This is the direct analogue of SQL's NOT IN over a generated sequence, and at these limits (at most 100 candidates) it is perfectly adequate.
s: Find MAX(customer_id) to fix the candidate range [1, mx].
For each i in 1..mx, test whether any row has customer_id equal to i.
Collect the values failing the test.
Return them ascending (natural if you iterate upward).
a.t: O(M·N) — up to M ≤ 100 candidate IDs each checked against N rows; negligible here.

a.i: Pay one pass over Customers to mark which IDs exist and track the maximum, then sweep 1..mx reading the marks. This replaces repeated table scans with an O(1) lookup per candidate — the same plan a database reaches with a hash anti-join. In pure SQL this is written with a recursive CTE generating the numbers and NOT IN filtering them.

Append i whenever it is unmarked.
Return the collected list ordered ascending.
a.t: O(N + M) — one pass over the rows plus one pass over the candidate range.

## Wrap-up

If asked in SQL, the canonical answer generates the candidate sequence with a recursive CTE and anti-joins it:

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE seq AS (
  SELECT 1 AS n
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1 FROM seq WHERE n < (SELECT MAX(customer_id) FROM Customers)
)
SELECT n AS ids
FROM seq
WHERE n NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM Customers)
ORDER BY ids;
```

**Pitfalls:** forgetting ORDER BY ids; terminating the recursion at a hardcoded constant instead of MAX(customer_id); off-by-one on the range (the maximum ID itself can never be missing); and using NOT IN against a nullable column, where NULL silently kills every comparison.

**Edge cases:** no gaps at all (empty result); IDs starting above 1 (nothing below the minimum is reported since the range starts at 1). **Follow-ups:** what if the ID domain were billions wide? Then generate only gap ranges between consecutive present IDs rather than individual rows.
